enrichment.short_title: Section 41 leave for other sexual abuse complaints

statutes_considered.title: Youth Justice and Criminal Evidence Act 1999

key_facts: Cooper and Betts were convicted at Nottingham Crown Court of indecency and indecent assault against children in their care, based largely on video interviews with twin complainants J and N.
The Crown adduced edited first video interviews; the defence sought to put before the jury other complaints made by J and N against third parties.
HHJ Benson restricted cross-examination about other complaints, treating much of it as questioning about complainants' sexual behaviour requiring leave under section 41.
Formal admissions told the jury that J and N had made complaints about sexual activity with adults other than the defendants.
The Court of Appeal viewed the full video interviews and held the convictions safe.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by leave of the single judge against conviction following trial at Nottingham Crown Court.
enrichment.ratio: Where a sexual offence trial turns on whether abuse occurred rather than consent, questioning about other unchallenged complaints of sexual abuse by complainants generally falls within section 41 as being about their sexual behaviour; absent a proper basis for suggesting such complaints were false, a trial judge may properly restrict cross-examination, and even if that were wrong the verdict would remain safe on the material before the jury.
legal_issues: Whether section 41 applied to cross-examination about other complaints of sexual abuse
Whether evidence of other complaints was admissible on credit or as inconsistent statements under the 1865 Act
Whether restriction of cross-examination rendered the trial unfair

enrichment.short_title: Unpleaded six-monthly compromises in tank dispute
key_facts: Huktra UK and Huktra NV, linked chemical transport companies, operated for years on oral agreements concerning tank carriage, cleaning, and powder equipment.
After their relationship ended in 1995-96, UK claimed return of retained tanks and NV counterclaimed for under-payment and over-charging exceeding £900,000.
UK pleaded a December 1995 compromise settling NV's under-payment claim against powder hire charges of £294,000.
The trial judge rejected the pleaded December 1995 compromise but found earlier six-monthly accord and satisfaction at accounting year ends down to June 1995.
NV appealed; UK cross-appealed on whether cleaning costs were chargeable at cost rather than commercial rates.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from the first liability judgment of HHJ Michael Kershaw QC sitting as a High Court judge.
enrichment.outcome: NV's appeal allowed; judge's six-monthly compromise findings set aside; UK's cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A judge cannot decide a case against a party on an alternative and inconsistent case of serial six-monthly compromises that was never pleaded, supported in witness statements, or argued at trial, even where some evidence of year-end discussions existed; separately, a judge may distinguish carriage and cleaning charges and find cleaning was invoiced at cost on the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the judge could find six-monthly compromises instead of the pleaded December 1995 compromise
Whether there was sufficient evidence for serial compromises
Whether cleaning costs between the parties were chargeable at cost or on a profit basis

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Wandsworth served an enforcement notice alleging a telecommunications mast exceeded the 15-metre permitted development height limit under Part 24 of the GPDO.
The operator had obtained a 1997 prior approval determination that prior approval was not required for a 15-metre monopole shown on submitted drawings including a headframe.
An inspector found the installed mast with headframe exceeded 15 metres but quashed the notice on estoppel because the built installation matched the notified drawings.
The council challenged the decision under the wrong statutory route and shortly after the House of Lords decision in Reprotech.
The Secretary of State conceded the inspector's estoppel reasoning could not be defended post-Reprotech.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review claim converted at hearing to permission to appeal under section 289 with extension of time; substantive challenge to inspector's enforcement appeal decision.
enrichment.outcome: Time extended; permission granted; appeal allowed; inspector's decision quashed and remitted for reconsideration.
enrichment.ratio: Private law estoppel cannot prevent a local planning authority exercising statutory enforcement powers; an inspector cannot lawfully allow an enforcement appeal on ground (c) while finding a breach of planning control and relying on estoppel rather than planning merits under ground (a); where the wrong challenge procedure was used, a short delay may be extended when merits are clear and prejudice is absent.
legal_issues: Whether estoppel barred enforcement after a prior notification determination
Whether the challenge should have been brought under section 288 or section 289
Whether time to appeal under section 289 should be extended
Effect of Reprotech on Western Fish estoppel reasoning

key_facts: A Colombian woman appealed refusal of asylum and removal directions after paramilitaries threatened her over suspected FARC links in Caloto.
The adjudicator accepted a well-founded fear in her home town but held she could internally relocate elsewhere in Colombia, including larger cities.
The Immigration Appeal Tribunal upheld that internal flight alternative finding and gave limited weight to UNHCR correspondence.
Fresh tribunal decisions and country material on Colombia internal relocation were relied on at the permission hearing.
Laws LJ granted permission to appeal, finding the tribunal's treatment of UNHCR material arguably exiguous.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal against Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision dismissing asylum appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; UNHCR to be notified and may submit limited written material.
enrichment.ratio: There is no rule of law that internal relocation is always unavailable in Colombia, but where a claimant has established a well-founded fear of persecution and substantial UNHCR and country evidence points to grave difficulties with internal relocation, it is arguable that a tribunal erred by insufficiently reasoning on that material and on inferences drawn from paramilitary conduct.
legal_issues: Whether the unduly harsh test from Robinson was misapplied
Whether the tribunal failed to take account of relevant country and UNHCR evidence
Whether internal relocation was available for this Colombian appellant

enrichment.short_title: Children's home use class C2 not C3 dwelling

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Use Classes) Order 1987

key_facts: Southern Childcare Limited used a semi-detached Barnstaple house to provide registered residential care for two children placed by local authorities.
Two non-resident staff provided continuous supervision on shifts; the property otherwise resembled an ordinary family house.
The company applied for a certificate of lawful use as a dwellinghouse under Class C3(b).
An inspector granted the certificate, treating non-resident carers as part of a single household with the children.
North Devon District Council appealed, arguing the use was Class C2 residential institution requiring resident carers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 289 against inspector's grant of lawful development certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; lawful use certificate upheld for this property on these facts.
enrichment.ratio: A small registered children's home with only non-resident shift carers is Class C2 residential institution rather than Class C3 dwellinghouse, because a single household for C3(b) requires resident carers capable of running the home; Sinclair was disapproved on that point, but even where use falls in C2 the change from prior C3 dwelling use was not material on the facts of this case.
legal_issues: Whether the use fell within Class C2 or Class C3 of the Use Classes Order
Whether non-resident carers could form part of a single household with residents
Whether there was a material change of use despite class reclassification

enrichment.short_title: Indemnity costs after Friskies particulars order

statutes_considered.title: Health and Safety at Work Act 1974

key_facts: Dudley MBC prosecuted Mr Bernard for Health and Safety at Work Act offences arising from building works at a care home.
The defendant's solicitors repeatedly sought Friskies-style particulars linking allegations to evidence; magistrates refused.
Lightman J ordered provision of a prosecution statement by 20 December 2002 or permission would be granted.
A prosecution schedule was eventually provided and the judicial review became academic, but costs remained in dispute.
The court found the prosecution case could not readily be understood from informations and statements alone.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review resolved after prosecution particulars supplied; hearing on costs only.
enrichment.outcome: Defendant awarded costs of judicial review and today's hearing on the indemnity basis, subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: In Health and Safety prosecutions a prosecuting authority must provide clear particulars, including aggravating features in writing per Friskies; steadfast refusal to do so may necessitate judicial review and warrants indemnity costs where conduct is unreasonably uncooperative even after belated compliance.
legal_issues: Whether prosecution particulars were adequate without a Friskies schedule
Whether judicial review costs should be awarded after particulars were supplied
Whether costs should be assessed on the standard or indemnity basis

enrichment.short_title: Fresh human rights claim after psychiatric decline
key_facts: Miss Ratnam, a Sri Lankan Tamil, claimed asylum on arrival in 1998; her claim and human rights appeal were dismissed in July 2001.
Dr Barakat's June 2001 report described stable paranoid schizophrenia managed with depot medication and brother's support.
A February 2002 report recorded marked deterioration, job loss, suicidal ideation, and high suicide risk if removed to Sri Lanka.
The Secretary of State treated the February representations as repetition of the rejected claim rather than a fresh human rights claim.
Permission was limited to whether the second report constituted a fresh claim and whether support-network error invalidated the decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Secretary of State refusal to treat February 2002 psychiatric evidence as a fresh human rights claim.
enrichment.outcome: November 2002 decision quashed; Secretary of State must consider February 2002 claim as fresh.
enrichment.ratio: Applying paragraph 346 by analogy, a later human rights claim based on a credible and significant psychiatric report documenting deterioration unavailable at the earlier appeal, including heightened suicide risk on removal, can be a fresh claim if it satisfies the Onibiyo acid test; it was irrational not to treat Dr Barakat's second report as such.
legal_issues: Whether Dr Barakat's second report constituted a fresh human rights claim
Whether paragraph 346 applies by analogy outside asylum
Whether the Secretary of State properly assessed suicide risk and support in Sri Lanka
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Manvinder Singh
Ademola Onibiyo v Secretary of State for the Home Department
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Ravichandran no 2

confidence.notes: Fresh claim analysis and quashing order are explicit; asylum issues were abandoned before final hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Bradford riot sentences reduced for some
key_facts: Fifteen defendants sentenced at Bradford Crown Court for riot or violent disorder during the Manningham riot of 7-8 July 2001.
The riot lasted about twelve hours, injured over 300 police officers, and caused damage estimated at £27 million.
Most defendants pleaded guilty and were identified from video footage; sentences for riot largely ranged from four to six-and-a-half years.
Judge Gullick said he was not concerned with the origins of the prolonged violence, which counsel argued skewed sentencing.
The Court of Appeal reduced sentences for Najeeb, Qazi, Maskin, and Shazad Ali but dismissed other appeals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals and renewed applications for leave to appeal against sentence following guilty pleas at Bradford Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Partial success: Najeeb and Shazad Ali reduced to three years; Qazi reduced to two years; Maskin granted leave and reduced to two years; other appeals dismissed or leave refused.
enrichment.ratio: For a riot of utmost gravity directed at police, deterrent custodial sentences were justified and starting points well above Keys were appropriate; however a blanket disregard of origins was wrong, and individual reductions were warranted where participation was limited, mental illness reduced culpability, or the violent-disorder offence merited a lower bracket.
legal_issues: Whether Bradford riot sentences were manifestly excessive
Whether origins of the riot were irrelevant to sentence
Appropriate starting points and guilty plea discounts where video evidence was overwhelming
Effect of mental illness on Qazi's sentence

enrichment.short_title: No prescriptive vehicular rights over common land

statutes_considered.title: Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000
Vehicular Access across Common and Other Land (England) Regulations 2002

key_facts: About 43 homeowners adjoining Newtown Common near Newbury had driven to the highway over the common for many years without owner permission.
Section 193 applied from 1928 by deed, making unauthorised carriage on the common a summary offence.
Bakewell Management sought declarations and injunctions, offering easements for payment.
Defendants claimed prescriptive vehicular easements by lost modern grant after twenty years' user.
The court held itself bound by Hanning v Top Deck Travel Group Ltd.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against declaration that defendants had no prescriptive vehicular rights over Newtown Common.
enrichment.ratio: An easement cannot be acquired by user that was at the time prohibited by a public statute passed for public benefit; driving carriages on common land under section 193(4) without lawful authority is such prohibited user, so lost modern grant and prescription do not operate, and Hanning remains binding on the Court of Appeal.
legal_issues: Whether vehicular easements can be acquired over section 193 common land by prescription or lost modern grant
Whether Hanning was decided per incuriam
Whether the owner could waive section 193 so as to permit grant of an easement
Effect of section 68 Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000
linked_authorities: Hanning v Top Deck Travel Group Ltd
Neaverson v Peterborough Rural District Council
George Legge & Son Ltd v Wenlock Corporation
R v Oxfordshire CC Ex P Sunningwell PC

enrichment.short_title: SEN tribunal erred on Essex Good Beginnings
key_facts: G, aged four, has autistic spectrum disorder with severely impaired speech and language.
Essex LEA maintained a statement providing its Good Beginnings programme; parents funded a private Lovaas programme costing about £28,000 per year.
The Special Educational Needs Tribunal rejected the parents' appeal, accepting both programmes could meet G's needs.
Essex Good Beginnings documentation required parents to implement and deliver agreed home programmes with key worker support.
Both parents refused to participate in delivering the Essex programme, preferring Lovaas.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal against Special Educational Needs Tribunal decision under section 11 of the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 framework.
enrichment.outcome: Tribunal decision quashed; matter remitted to tribunal.
enrichment.ratio: An LEA cannot lawfully specify special educational provision that depends on parents themselves delivering teaching or implementing programmes; where parents will not do so, the Essex Good Beginnings scheme fails to satisfy the LEA's personal duty under section 324(5)(a) to arrange the specified provision.
legal_issues: Whether Essex Good Beginnings unlawfully imposed parental delivery of special education
Whether the LEA discharged its duty under section 324(5)(a) where parents refused cooperation
Whether the tribunal erred in approving the statement
